title: New Superconductor Breaks 30-Year Record at Ambient Pressure
summary: A team at the University of Houston has shattered a three-decade-old record in superconductivity, achieving zero electrical resistance at 151 Kelvin (-122°C) under ambient pressure. The advance, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, could pave the way for more efficient power grids, advanced medical imaging, and fusion energy. Superconductors are materials that conduct electricity without energy loss, but most require extreme cooling to near absolute zero. The previous ambient-pressure record of 133 Kelvin (-140°C) was set in 1993 with a mercury-based ceramic. The new material, developed by physicists Ching-Wu Chu and Liangzi Deng, pushes the transition temperature 18 degrees higher. "Transmitting electricity in the grid loses about 8% of the electricity," said Chu, a pioneer in high-temperature superconductivity. "If we conserve that energy, that's billions of dollars of savings and reduces environmental impacts." The key to the breakthrough is a technique called pressure quenching. The researchers first subjected the material to intense pressure, which enhanced its superconducting properties. Then, while maintaining a low temperature, they rapidly removed the pressure. This process "trapped" the material in a metastable state, preserving the high-pressure superconducting phase at normal conditions. "Our method shows that it is possible to retain that state without maintaining pressure," Chu explained. The achievement is particularly significant because ambient-pressure operation makes superconductors far more accessible for research and practical applications. Cooling systems for conventional superconductors are bulky and expensive; eliminating the need for high pressure is a major step toward real-world use. While room-temperature superconductivity (around 300 Kelvin) remains a distant goal, this record narrows the gap to about 140 degrees. The researchers are optimistic that further refinements could yield even higher transition temperatures. The work builds on decades of progress, including Chu's own 1987 discovery of a superconductor at 93 Kelvin, which sparked a global race. Now, with pressure quenching, the field may be entering a new era of stable, high-temperature superconductors.
why_it_matters: This breakthrough brings us closer to a future where electricity can be transmitted without waste, potentially saving billions of dollars and reducing the environmental footprint of energy grids and medical technology—directly affecting the infrastructure students will inherit.

background_read: Superconductivity was first discovered in 1911 when mercury was cooled to near absolute zero (0 K / -273°C). For decades, all known superconductors worked only at extremely low temperatures.

In 1986, a breakthrough came when scientists found ceramic materials that became superconducting at higher temperatures, earning a Nobel Prize. This sparked a global race, and in 1987, Ching-Wu Chu (now at the University of Houston) discovered a material that worked at 93 Kelvin, above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen.
The previous ambient-pressure record of 133 Kelvin was set in 1993 using a mercury-based ceramic called HgBa₂Ca₂Cu₃O₈, and it remained unbroken for 30 years until this new study.

Most high-temperature superconductors require enormous pressure to work—sometimes millions of times atmospheric pressure—which makes them impractical for widespread use. The pressure quenching technique traps the high-pressure structure at normal conditions.

If room-temperature superconductivity (about 300 Kelvin) is ever achieved at ambient pressure, it could revolutionize power grids, making electricity transmission lossless, and improve technologies like MRI machines, maglev trains, and fusion reactors.

perspectives.description: Shattering a 30-year record at ambient pressure is a huge step toward practical superconductors. This opens the door for more accessible research and could accelerate the development of lossless power lines, smaller MRI machines, and powerful magnets for fusion energy.

The superconducting temperature is still extremely cold (-122°C), requiring liquid nitrogen or other coolants. Real-world applications may remain costly and complex. Past claims of room-temperature superconductors have sometimes been retracted, so cautious optimism is needed.

The history of superconductivity is marked by long plateaus and sudden jumps. The pressure quenching method represents a new strategy to create metastable states, which could be applied to other materials. However, fundamental physics still limits how high transition temperatures can go in these ceramics.

The team plans to refine the material further, hoping to raise the transition temperature even higher. If the approach can be scaled to industrial production, it might finally move superconductors from laboratory curiosities to components of everyday energy and medical systems.
